lessons.title: Assessing venues: community halls, hotels, gardens, and family compounds
lessons.body:
When a client asks you to plan an event, the first step is to assess the venue. In many African communities, you have four main options: community halls, hotels, gardens, and family compounds. Each has strengths and weaknesses. Community halls are affordable, often located in the heart of the neighbourhood, and have basic facilities like toilets and a kitchen. But they may lack air conditioning, have old wiring, or be booked out months in advance. Hotels offer convenienceâtables, chairs, power, and catering are usually includedâbut they are expensive and may restrict outside decor or food. Gardens are beautiful and flexible, but you must check for uneven ground, lack of shade, and no backup power. Family compounds are personal and free, but space may be tight, and you may need to rent everything from chairs to generators.

Start your assessment with a site visit. Bring a notebook, a tape measure, and your phone for photos. Check access: Can a truck deliver chairs and a tent? Is there a gate wide enough? Are there stairs? Look at power: How many sockets? What is the voltage? In many African countries, it's 220-240V. Ask about water: Is there a tap? Toilets? For gardens, check the soilâis it muddy after rain? For compounds, ask about noise restrictions and neighbours.

Talk to the venue manager or owner. Ask about booking fees, deposit, cancellation policy, and any rules about decorations, cooking, or music. Get everything in writing, even if it's a simple handwritten agreement. For hotels, confirm if they charge corkage for outside drinks or if they require their own caterers. For community halls, find out if there is a caretaker who will be present and if you need to pay them separately.

Finally, consider the guest experience. Is the venue easy to find? Is there parking? For elderly guests, are there ramps? For a wedding in a garden, is there a backup plan if it rains? Once you have assessed all options, compare them against the client's budget and needs. A good event planner always has a Plan B venue in mind.

lessons.title: Measuring spaces and planning seating arrangements
lessons.body:
Measuring a venue accurately saves you from the embarrassment of too few chairs or a cramped dance floor. You need a tape measure (at least 30 metres), a notebook, and a helper. Start by measuring the length and width of the main area. For a rectangular hall, multiply length by width to get square metres. For example, a hall 15m long and 10m wide is 150 square metres. But usable space is less after you subtract for pillars, stage, buffet area, and walkways.

For seating, the rule of thumb: allow 1.2 to 1.5 square metres per person for theatre-style (chairs in rows) and 1.5 to 2 square metres per person for banquet-style (round tables with chairs). So a 150 square metre hall can seat about 100 people at round tables (150 Ã· 1.5 = 100) or 125 in rows (150 Ã· 1.2 = 125). But always round down to be safe. For a wedding with a dance floor, reserve at least 3m x 3m. For a buffet, allow 2m x 4m. For a stage, 4m x 3m.

Measure doorways and corridors. A standard chair is 45cm wide; a round table for 8 is 1.5m diameter. Can you fit them through the door? If not, you may need to assemble inside. Also measure ceiling height for decorations like drapes or chandeliers. In many African halls, ceiling height is 3-4 metres; in tents, it's 2.5-3 metres.

Draw a simple floor plan on graph paper. Mark the entrance, stage, dance floor, buffet, cake table, gift table, and seating. Use a scale like 1cm = 1m. Then place your tables and chairs. For round tables, leave 1.2m between tables for chairs and walking. For rows, leave 0.8m between rows for legs. Don't forget a aisle for the bridal party. Share this plan with your client and the venue manager. Adjust as needed. A good plan prevents chaos on the day.

lessons.title: Coordinating with venue managers for access and rules
lessons.body:
The venue manager is your key partner. Whether it's a community hall caretaker or a hotel events coordinator, you must coordinate access, rules, and timing. Start by scheduling a meeting at least two weeks before the event. Bring your floor plan, a list of equipment, and your timeline. Ask these questions: When can we access the venue for setup? How long before the event? Can we come the day before? What time must we leave after the event? Is there a security deposit? What are the rules about noise, cooking, and decorations?

For access, get the name and phone number of the person who will open the gate. Confirm if there is a loading bay or if you must carry items from the street. In many African cities, parking is tight, so ask if you can reserve space for your delivery truck. If the venue is a hotel, they may require you to use their suppliers for power or AV. Clarify any fees for early access or overtime.

Rules vary. Some halls forbid nails in walls, so you must use tape or stands for banners. Some gardens prohibit open flames, so you need LED candles. Some compounds have curfewsâmusic must stop by 10pm. Write down all rules and share them with your team. Also ask about existing furniture: tables, chairs, and kitchen equipment. If they provide chairs, inspect them for damage. If you bring your own, label them with your business name.

On the setup day, arrive early and do a walkthrough with the manager. Confirm power points, water taps, and toilet locations. Ask where you can store empty boxes and rubbish. Establish a contact person for emergencies. After the event, do a joint inspection to avoid deposit disputes. Leave the venue clean and take photos as proof. Good coordination builds trust and leads to repeat bookings.

lessons.title: Planning for power, water, and backup generators
lessons.body:
Power and water are the lifelines of any event. Without them, you can't run lights, sound, or catering. In many African venues, grid power is unreliable, so you must plan for backup. First, calculate your power needs. List all equipment: sound system (500-2000W), lights (1000-3000W), fridge (200W), fans (100W each), phone chargers (negligible). Add them up. For a medium wedding, you might need 5-8 kilowatts (kW).

Check the venue's power supply. Look at the main breaker box. Is it 220V or 240V? How many circuits? A standard socket in Africa provides 13-15 amps, which is about 3kW. So you may need multiple sockets or a distribution board. If the venue has a generator, ask its capacity and fuel level. If not, rent one. A 10kW diesel generator costs about $100-$200 per day in many African cities, plus fuel. Fuel consumption is roughly 1 litre per hour per 3kW. So a 10kW generator uses about 3 litres per hour. For an 8-hour event, that's 24 litres.

Water: For a garden event, you need water for drinking, cooking, and toilets. Ask if there is a tap and if it's potable. If not, buy bottled water or a water tank. A 1000-litre tank can serve 200 guests for a day. For toilets, rent portable toilets if the venue has none. One toilet per 50 guests is a good rule.

Backup plan: Always have a generator as backup, even if the venue has grid power. Test it before the event. Bring extra fuel, extension cables (at least 30 metres), and power strips. Label cables to avoid tripping. For sound, use a voltage stabiliser to protect equipment. For lighting, use LED bulbs to save power. Assign a team member to monitor power throughout the event. If the generator fails, have a mechanic on call. A well-powered event runs smoothly and keeps guests comfortable.

lessons.title: Setting up decor within time limits and with a small team
lessons.body:
Decor transforms a plain venue into a memorable space, but you must work fast and smart. With a small team of 2-4 people, you need a plan. Start by creating a setup schedule. For a typical wedding, you might have 4 hours to set up. Divide tasks: one person handles drapes and backdrops, another does table settings, another arranges flowers and centrepieces, and you supervise and handle lighting.

Use the right tools: a step ladder, a staple gun (if allowed), zip ties, fishing line, double-sided tape, and a glue gun. For African fabric decor, use kitenge or ankara cloths. They are colourful and lightweight. Measure the backdrop area and cut fabric in advance. For a 6m x 3m backdrop, you need about 6 metres of fabric (if 1.5m wide, you need 4 panels). Attach with zip ties to a frame or use a curtain rod.

For table settings, work in batches. Set up all tables with tablecloths first, then plates, then centrepieces. Use a trolley or cart to move items. For a small team, avoid heavy liftingâuse a dolly for chairs and tables. If you have 20 round tables, each with 8 chairs, that's 160 chairs. Two people can move 20 chairs per trip with a dolly, so 8 trips. It takes about 30 minutes.

Time limits: Always add 30 minutes buffer. If setup starts at 10am and event is at 2pm, aim to finish by 1:30pm. Assign one person to do a final walkthrough at 1pm. Check for missing items, crooked tablecloths, and burnt-out bulbs. Keep a toolkit with spare bulbs, tape, and scissors. After the event, tear down quickly. Pack items in labelled boxes. With a small team, you can set up a 100-guest event in 3-4 hours if you are organised. Practice makes perfect.

lessons.title: Handling weather challenges for outdoor events
lessons.body:
Outdoor events in Africa face sun, rain, wind, and dust. You must plan for all. First, check the weather forecast a week before and again the day before. In many regions, rainy seasons are predictableâe.g., April to June in East Africa. If rain is likely, rent a tent. A 10m x 20m tent can cover 200 guests. Cost: $500-$1000 per day. Ensure the tent has side walls and a floor. For sun, provide shade with umbrellas or a canopy. For wind, secure tents with ropes and stakes. In dusty areas, water the ground before the event.

Have a rain plan. If it starts raining, move the ceremony to the tent or indoors. Assign team members to guide guests. Keep plastic sheets to cover sound equipment and chairs. For mud, lay down wooden pallets or mats as walkways. For heat, provide water stations and fans. In hot climates, schedule events for early morning or late afternoon.

For wind, avoid lightweight decor like paper lanterns. Use weighted bases for centrepieces. Secure tablecloths with clips. For dust, cover food and keep serving dishes closed. If the venue is a garden, ask if you can use their lawnâif it's waterlogged, you may need to relocate.

Communicate with guests. Send a message if the event is delayed or moved. Have a backup indoor venue as a last resort. On the day, monitor the sky. If clouds darken, start moving things early. After the event, dry all equipment before storing to prevent mould. Weather is unpredictable, but with a solid plan, you can handle anything. Always have a Plan B and C.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a key advantage of a community hall as a venue?
options: B) It often has modern air conditioning
C) It is affordable and centrally located
quiz.explanation: Community halls are known for being affordable and often located in the heart of the neighbourhood.

quiz.q: When assessing a garden venue, what should you check regarding the ground?
options: B) If it is uneven or muddy after rain
C) If it has artificial grass
quiz.explanation: Gardens can have uneven ground and become muddy after rain, which affects setup and guest comfort.

quiz.q: What is the recommended square metres per person for banquet-style seating?
quiz.explanation: Banquet-style seating with round tables requires about 1.5 to 2 square metres per person.

quiz.q: Why is it important to measure doorways and corridors when planning seating?
options: A) To determine the number of chairs needed
B) To ensure tables and chairs can fit through
C) To calculate the dance floor size
D) To decide on the colour scheme
quiz.explanation: Measuring doorways ensures that large items like tables and chairs can be moved into the venue.

quiz.q: What is a good rule for spacing between round tables?
quiz.explanation: Leave about 1.2 metres between round tables to allow for chairs and walking space.

quiz.q: When coordinating with a venue manager, what should you get in writing?
options: B) All rules, fees, and access times
quiz.explanation: Getting all rules, fees, and access times in writing prevents misunderstandings.

quiz.q: What should you ask about regarding power when assessing a venue?
options: A) The number of light bulbs
B) The voltage and number of sockets
C) The colour of the power cables
D) The brand of the generator
quiz.explanation: Knowing the voltage and number of sockets helps you plan for your equipment's power needs.

quiz.q: Why is it important to confirm the name of the person who will open the gate?
options: A) To send them a gift
B) To ensure smooth access for setup
C) To invite them to the event
D) To ask about parking fees
quiz.explanation: Having a contact for gate access ensures your team can enter without delays.

quiz.q: What is a common rule in some venues regarding decorations?
quiz.explanation: Many venues forbid nails in walls to prevent damage, so you must use alternatives like tape or stands.

quiz.q: How can you calculate the power needs for an event?
options: A) Guess based on the number of guests
B) List all equipment and add up their wattage
D) Use a standard 5kW for any event
quiz.explanation: Listing all equipment and summing their wattage gives an accurate estimate of power needs.

quiz.q: What is the typical fuel consumption of a 10kW generator per hour?
quiz.explanation: A 10kW generator consumes about 3 litres of fuel per hour.

quiz.q: Why is it important to have a voltage stabiliser for sound equipment?
options: A) To make the sound louder
B) To protect equipment from power surges
quiz.explanation: Voltage stabilisers protect sensitive sound equipment from voltage fluctuations.

quiz.q: How many portable toilets are recommended for 200 guests?
quiz.explanation: A common rule is one toilet per 50 guests, so for 200 guests you need 4 toilets.

quiz.q: What is a good practice when setting up decor with a small team?
options: B) Assign specific tasks to each person
quiz.explanation: Assigning specific tasks improves efficiency and ensures all areas are covered.

quiz.q: What tool is useful for attaching fabric backdrops without damaging walls?
options: B) Zip ties and fishing line
quiz.explanation: Zip ties and fishing line are gentle and effective for attaching fabric without nails.

quiz.q: Why should you add a 30-minute buffer to your setup schedule?
options: A) To allow for unexpected delays
D) To test the sound system
quiz.explanation: A buffer accounts for unforeseen issues that could delay setup.

quiz.q: What is a key consideration for outdoor events during the rainy season?
options: B) Rent a tent with side walls
quiz.explanation: A tent with side walls provides protection from rain and wind.

quiz.q: How can you handle dust at an outdoor event?
options: A) Water the ground before the event
quiz.explanation: Watering the ground helps settle dust and keeps the air clean.

quiz.q: What should you do if it starts raining during an outdoor event?
options: B) Move guests to a tent or indoors
quiz.explanation: Moving guests to a covered area ensures their comfort and safety.

quiz.q: Why is it important to dry equipment after an outdoor event?
options: A) To prevent rust and mould
D) To return it to the rental company
quiz.explanation: Drying equipment prevents rust and mould, extending its lifespan.

quiz.q: What is the first step in assessing a venue?
quiz.explanation: A site visit allows you to see the venue's condition and take measurements.

quiz.q: Which venue type often includes tables, chairs, and power in the price?
quiz.explanation: Hotels typically provide furniture and power as part of their package.

quiz.q: What is a good way to remember the layout of a venue?
options: A) Draw a floor plan to scale
quiz.explanation: A scaled floor plan helps you plan seating and decor accurately.

quiz.q: How many chairs can two people move per trip using a dolly?
quiz.explanation: With a dolly, two people can move about 20 chairs per trip efficiently.

quiz.q: What should you bring to a venue assessment?
options: A) A tape measure and notebook
quiz.explanation: A tape measure and notebook are essential for recording measurements and notes.

quiz.q: What is a common fee associated with hotels for outside drinks?
quiz.explanation: Hotels often charge a corkage fee if you bring your own drinks.

quiz.q: Why is it important to label your equipment?
options: A) To identify it as yours
B) To make it look nice
quiz.explanation: Labelling helps prevent loss or mix-up with the venue's equipment.

quiz.q: What is a good source of power backup for an event?
quiz.explanation: Diesel generators are commonly used as reliable backup power for events.

quiz.q: How much water should you plan per guest for drinking and cooking?
quiz.explanation: A common estimate is 5 litres per guest for drinking and cooking needs.

quiz.q: What is a key benefit of using LED bulbs for event lighting?
options: A) They are cheaper to buy
quiz.explanation: LED bulbs consume less power, reducing the load on generators.
